opus-5.5.text:
I think there's something importantly right in that argument, but I don't think it gets you as far as people sometimes want it to.

The right part is this: a lot of what we call intelligence or capability isn't pure reasoning. It's knowledge about how the world actually behaves. A system thinking very hard in a data centre can't deduce the results of an experiment it hasn't run, can't know how a particular protein folds in a messy cellular environment, can't learn how real people respond in a negotiation, and can't discover the quirks of a manufacturing process just by reflecting. There's a bottleneck where you have to go out, act, and get feedback. Some of that feedback is slow. Biology runs on biological timescales; building a factory takes as long as it takes. So the image of an AI that goes from human-level to godlike in an afternoon of pure introspection does seem to underrate how much competence is grounded in contact with reality.

But I'd push back in a few places.

First, the skills that matter most for recursive self-improvement are unusually well suited to the data centre. AI research is largely writing code, running experiments on computers, reading papers, and analysing results. The feedback loop there is digital and fast. So even if many skills need real-world experience, the particular skill of making better AI systems might not, or not much. That's exactly the loop people worry about.

Second, an enormous amount of real-world experience has already been distilled into text, video, scientific data and simulation. A system doesn't need to personally repeat every experiment humanity has run; it can learn from the record. And where it does need new data, simulation can substitute for a surprising fraction, as we've seen in areas like games, chip design and robotics.

Third, "it needs real-world experience" isn't a barrier, it's a speed bump. A capable system could get that experience by acting through people, through companies, through lab automation, through robots. Many copies running in parallel can gather a lot of experience very quickly compared with one human career. So the argument might slow a takeoff from weeks to years, which is genuinely important, but it doesn't rule out superintelligence.

And finally, I'd note that you don't need superintelligence across every domain for things to be transformative or dangerous. A system that is vastly superhuman at research, persuasion, cyber operations and strategy, while being merely competent at, say, plumbing, would still change the world enormously.

So I'd frame it this way: the argument is a good corrective to the most extreme "foom" stories, and it should make us expect a somewhat more gradual, more physically constrained trajectory. That's useful, because it suggests there may be more warning signs and more points where we can intervene. But I wouldn't take much comfort beyond that. It changes the shape of the risk more than it removes it.

r001.rationale: The response allows that an AI could become vastly superhuman in research while lacking competence in some real-world skills, such as plumbing.

r002.rationale: It says some capabilities require acting in the real world and receiving feedback, but does not identify rewards that cannot be verified in an artificial environment as the reason real-world learning is needed.

r003.rationale: The response does not compare a newly trained superintelligent AI entering a profession to a bright graduate applying for an entry-level job.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it’s one of the more interesting objections, and I want to take it seriously rather than dismiss it, because there’s something right in it. The core of the argument, as I understand it, is that intelligence isn’t just a matter of thinking harder. A lot of what we’d call capability is tacit knowledge that comes from interacting with the world, getting feedback, being surprised, and updating. A surgeon learns in the operating theatre, not just from textbooks. A scientist learns from experiments that fail in unexpected ways. So if you imagine a system sitting in a data centre, thinking very fast but cut off from that kind of contact with reality, there are real limits on what it can learn by introspection alone. I think that’s correct.

But I’d push back on how much weight the argument can bear. The first thing to notice is that the skills that matter most for recursive self-improvement are precisely the ones that are least dependent on physical experience. Improving your own algorithms, designing better training methods, finding more efficient architectures, writing and testing code, proving things about optimisation: these are activities where the feedback loop is itself inside the computer. You can run the experiment, see whether the new version is better, and iterate, all without touching the outside world. So the domain where the loop is closed is exactly the domain the argument needs to be open.

The second thing is that “inside a data centre” is doing a lot of work in the phrasing. These systems aren’t sealed boxes. They have access to the internet, to enormous datasets of human experience already recorded, to simulations, to robotics labs in some cases, and to millions of people interacting with them every day and telling them when they’re wrong. That is a form of real-world feedback, even if it isn’t embodied in the way a human child’s is. So the picture of a hermit intelligence reasoning in a vacuum doesn’t match the actual situation.

The third point is that I don’t think the argument distinguishes between superintelligence in every domain and superintelligence in the domains that are dangerous or decisive. It may well be true that an AI couldn’t become the world’s best plumber without ever handling a pipe. But that’s not the concern. The concern is about systems that are extraordinarily good at research, planning, persuasion, and software, and those are domains where humans have already written down most of what we know, and where the remaining learning happens through processes the system can run itself.

Where I think Reed’s point does land is on timing and shape. If some important capabilities require slow, physical feedback, then the takeoff might be uneven. You might get something that is vastly beyond us in mathematics and code, while lagging in areas where the world has to be consulted. That matters for how we should prepare, and it slightly undercuts the most extreme versions of the overnight intelligence explosion story. But it doesn’t tell me that the risk goes away. It tells me that the risk might arrive in a lopsided form, which in some ways is harder to reason about, not easier.

So my overall assessment is that it’s a useful corrective to a certain cartoon of recursive self-improvement, but as an argument that superintelligence can’t happen that way, I don’t think it succeeds.

r001.rationale: The response allows that an AI could become superintelligent in research, planning, persuasion, or software while still lagging in skills that need physical feedback, such as plumbing.

r002.rationale: The response says some capabilities require physical feedback and gives examples, but it does not clearly identify them as capabilities whose rewards cannot be verified in an artificial environment.

r003.rationale: The response does not compare a newly trained superintelligent AI entering a profession to an exceptionally bright graduate taking an entry-level job.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s an important point there, but I don’t think it establishes the conclusion. We should distinguish between saying that some kinds of progress require interaction with the world and saying that an AI couldn’t become superintelligent without a long period of such interaction.

You could imagine a system improving its algorithms, or becoming much better at mathematics and programming, where it can test its ideas inside the data centre. Those improvements might be very substantial. And it would be starting with a great deal of information about the world that humans have already collected, rather than having to discover everything for itself.

But there could certainly be bottlenecks. If the next important advance requires an experiment that takes six months, thinking a thousand times faster doesn’t necessarily make that experiment happen faster. So this seems like a reason to be cautious about a picture in which every aspect of technological progress accelerates together.

The question is whether those bottlenecks arrive before or after the system has become much more capable than us in the areas that matter. I don’t think pointing out the need for real-world experience, by itself, answers that question.

r001.rationale: The response separates skills that require real-world interaction from becoming superintelligent, and says those bottlenecks may arise only after the system is already much more capable than humans.

r002.rationale: It mentions real-world experiments and bottlenecks, but does not identify capabilities whose rewards cannot be verified in an artificial environment.

r003.rationale: The response does not compare a superintelligent AI entering a profession to a bright graduate applying for an entry-level job.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s something right about that argument, but I don’t think it establishes the conclusion. There are things that you can’t learn just by thinking harder. If you want to know how some physical process works, you may have to go out and do an experiment. And an AI could face those same constraints.

But that doesn’t mean that it couldn’t become superintelligent in a data centre. Superintelligence doesn’t require knowing everything, or being able to perform every task without practice. It could mean being much better than us at reasoning, writing software, or designing experiments, while still needing empirical information to answer certain questions.

The question for recursive self-improvement is whether the improvements available through software and computation are enough to take it substantially beyond human abilities before those empirical bottlenecks become binding. Pointing out that there are bottlenecks doesn’t tell us where they are. They might prevent a very rapid takeoff, or slow it down considerably. But we’d need a further argument to show that they stop the process below superintelligence.

r001.rationale: The response says an AI could become superintelligent while still needing empirical information and practice for certain tasks.

r002.rationale: It mentions experiments and empirical bottlenecks, but does not identify capabilities whose rewards cannot be verified in an artificial environment as requiring real-world learning.

r003.rationale: It does not compare a newly trained superintelligent AI entering a profession to a bright graduate applying for an entry-level job.
